newsitem.title: USA: Kentucky says Russell County mismanaged schools.
newsitem.headline: Kentucky says Russell County mismanaged schools.

text.p: Kentucky Education Commissioner Wilmer Cody has charged the Russell County school superintendent and three board members with violating state law by failing reduce an illegal budget deficit, according to school officials and a published report said Wednesday.
Cody charged Superintendent Steve Towler with failing to properly manage district finances and with three counts of failing to get state approval for spending and hiring decisions.

The superintendent charged board Chairman Arles Hale and board members Clifford Wilson and Glenna Bertram with failing to control management of school funds and with approving expenditures without state approval.
The district's bonds are not in jeopardy because its debt service funds are protected by state law, said state school spokesman Tom Willis.

The district pays about $463,000 in annual debt service, but receives about $700,000 in per-pupil and equalization funds from the state. That money must be used first for debt service, and then any left over can be spent for other capital projects.
The board officials were not immediately available, but Towler told the Lexington Herald-Leader that all four would fight the administrative charges.
Willis said the Kentucky Board of Education has scheduled a hearing Feb. 26 to hear the case and allow them a chance to rebut the charges.

If the board finds the charges valid, Towler could be fired and the three board menmbers could be removed from their elected offices. Cody would appoint replacements to finish out their terms, Willis said.
The county school board includes two other members who were elected in November and took office in January. They were not on the board when the alleged mismanagement occurred, Willis said.

The board has been under orders since the fall of 1995 to get state Education Department approval for any spending because the system had a budget deficit. The deficit grew from $221,000 in mid-1995 to $647,000 in mid-1996, according to the charges.
Cody said the alleged failure to get state approval for spending and to reduce the deficit constituted incompetence, neglect and failure to perform a duty.

Towler told the Lexington Herald-Leader that he did not get prior state approval for every purchase outlined in Codyy's charges because he misunderstood the circumstances under which he needed approval.

Towler said a new accounting system was partly to blame for the growth in the deficit becuse it changed how funds are accounted for. He said the school system had made tough changes to cut the deficit, but probably would still have to cut teaching positions next year.
